title: May Day
hook: many countries honor workers on 1 May or in early September

segments.voice: Yesterday, lila and play is work: the tower of blocks, and the city full of children playing. Your line was play. Did you get your ten minutes? Today, a day set aside for the grown-ups who do the work. Day nine hundred thirty.

A cup of morning coffee passes through more hands than anyone drinking it will ever meet. Someone picked the beans. Someone drove the truck. Someone stocked the shelf, someone fixed the pipe that brings the water, someone cleaned the floor of the shop before it opened. Their faces aren't on the cup, and their names aren't on the receipt. In a number of countries, there's one day a year that tries to fix that. In some it falls on the first of May. In the United States and Canada, it's Labor Day, in early September. Today: May Day.
screen: `MORE HANDS THAN YOU'LL MEET.` → `NO NAMES ON THE CUP.` → `A DAY FOR THE WORKERS.`

segments.voice: First, the day itself. Workers' days are marked in different ways: parades, speeches, a day off, a cookout at the end of summer. Some are political, some just restful. Whatever the style, the idea underneath is simple. The people who do the work should be seen. Second, an old law about wages. The book of Leviticus sets a rule about hired workers. In the King James words: "the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning." Pay the day laborer the same day. Deuteronomy explains why: he is poor, and he has set his heart on it. A day's wage held back overnight is a family's dinner held back. Third, a teaching in Islam. A hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, reported in Ibn Majah, says, in paraphrase: give the worker his wages before his sweat dries. Not next month. Not after the paperwork. Before the sweat dries. Two traditions, two different books, the same urgency about the person who did the work. Fourth, a saint in an apron. The Catholic Church keeps the first of May as a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, the carpenter of Nazareth. So on the same day some streets fill with banners, some churches remember a man with sawdust on his sleeves. What these share is a turn of attention. The finished thing, the coffee, the clean floor, the working pipe, is easy to see. The hands that made it are easy to miss. A workers' day is a day for looking past the thing to the hands.
screen: `THE PEOPLE WHO WORK, SEEN.` · `PAY BEFORE THE MORNING.` · `BEFORE HIS SWEAT DRIES.` · `SAINT JOSEPH THE WORKER.` · then, large: `MAY DAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Choose one ordinary thing you've used today: a cup, a light switch, a bus seat, the food in your fridge. Hold it in your mind. Now trace it backward, one pair of hands at a time. Who made it, who moved it, who kept it working, who cleaned up after. You won't know their names. Just let them be there, one after another. Then choose one worker you will actually see today, and decide how you'll thank them. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
May Day. A day for honoring workers, kept on the first of May in some countries and in early September in others. Today's word.

Your line: thank the workers. Today, thank one worker out loud, by name if you know it: the driver, the cleaner, the cashier, the person who fixed something. Look up when you say it. Day nine hundred thirty.

howItsDone: On workers' days, people take part in parades and gatherings, take a day off, or simply rest; some Catholics keep 1 May as the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker.
